title: Production Monitoring and Observability
subtitle: Knowledge Check
intro: Check your understanding of Module 6: Production Monitoring and Observability. Pick an answer for each question and submit. Correct answers are confirmed; for a wrong answer you get a hint (the right answer is not revealed) and you try again until you get it right.

questions.prompt: A development team has deployed an agentic AI application using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The team needs to monitor the agent's performance and troubleshoot issues in production. They want to understand the complete flow of user interactions, including which tools are being called and how the agent is making decisions. Which approach should they implement?
options: Enable AWS X-Ray tracing and set up custom CloudWatch metrics for each agent component
Configure AgentCore Observability with OpenTelemetry instrumentation to capture sessions, traces, and spans
Implement custom logging for each agent component and store logs in Amazon S3
Deploy Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries to simulate user interactions with the agent
questions.answer: Configure AgentCore Observability with OpenTelemetry instrumentation to capture sessions, traces, and spans
questions.why: The correct answer is B: configure AgentCore Observability with OpenTelemetry instrumentation to capture sessions, traces, and spans. Let's review why. Option A, enabling X-Ray tracing and setting up custom CloudWatch metrics for each component, is incorrect, because while X-Ray provides distributed tracing, it isn't purpose-built for the hierarchical session, trace, and span structure that agents need. Option B is correct, because AgentCore Observability with OpenTelemetry instrumentation provides comprehensive monitoring through CloudWatch and captures the full hierarchy of sessions, traces, spans, and sub-spans, giving visibility into reasoning steps, tool invocations, and model interactions, which is exactly what's needed to understand decision-making and troubleshoot. Option C, custom logging to Amazon S3, is incorrect, because it would require significant development effort and wouldn't provide structured visibility into decision-making. And option D, CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, is incorrect, because canaries test availability and performance but don't provide detailed visibility into agent reasoning and tool invocations.

questions.prompt: Which view in the CloudWatch Generative AI Observability dashboard provides information about individual agent metrics, AgentCore Runtime metrics, and a list of sessions?
options: Agents view
Agent detail view
Session detail view
Trace detail view
questions.why: The correct answer is B: the Agent detail view. Let's review why. Option A, the Agents view, is incorrect, because it provides an overview of all agents rather than detailed metrics for an individual agent. Option B is correct, because the Agent detail view, which you reach by selecting an individual agent from the Agents view, provides that agent's individual metrics, its AgentCore Runtime metrics, and a list of its sessions, including metrics like session and trace counts, foundation model token usage, system and client errors, errors and latency by span, throttles, and authentication metrics. Option C, the Session detail view, is incorrect, because it shows details about a specific session, not individual agent metrics. And option D, the Trace detail view, is incorrect, because it shows information about specific traces, not individual agent metrics.

questions.prompt: Which option correctly orders and defines the AgentCore Observability hierarchy from broadest to most granular?
options: A span contains traces, which contain sessions.
A trace represents an entire multi-conversation user journey, while a session is one request-and-response cycle.
A session (the complete user conversation) contains traces (each a single request-and-response cycle), which contain spans (discrete units of work), which can contain sub-spans (steps within a span).
Spans and traces are the same thing, with no nesting relationship between them.
questions.answer: A session (the complete user conversation) contains traces (each a single request-and-response cycle), which contain spans (discrete units of work), which can contain sub-spans (steps within a span).
questions.why: The correct answer is C: a session, the complete user conversation, contains traces, each a single request-and-response cycle, which contain spans, discrete units of work, which can contain sub-spans, steps within a span. Let's review why. Option A is incorrect, because it inverts the hierarchy; sessions are the broadest unit and spans are among the most granular, not the other way around. Option B is incorrect, because it swaps the definitions: a trace is a single request-and-response cycle, while a session is the complete user conversation or interaction context. Option C is correct, because it matches the module's definitions exactly, from the broad session, through the per-request trace, down to the span as the most granular measurable unit of work, with sub-spans nesting inside a parent span to track individual steps. Option D is incorrect, because spans and traces are distinct: spans nest within traces, and sub-spans nest within spans.

questions.prompt: A team is enabling production observability for a self-hosted agent. Which combination of requirements does the module specify?
options: Add the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry package to the requirements file, launch the agent with the opentelemetry-instrument command, activate CloudWatch Transaction Search, and grant IAM access to CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, and X-Ray.
Simply enable a checkbox in the Bedrock console, with no code or package changes required.
Install a proprietary AWS-only tracing agent instead of OpenTelemetry.
No IAM permissions are required, because Observability runs outside your account.
questions.answer: Add the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry package to the requirements file, launch the agent with the opentelemetry-instrument command, activate CloudWatch Transaction Search, and grant IAM access to CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, and X-Ray.
questions.why: The correct answer is A: add the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry package to the requirements file, launch the agent with the opentelemetry-instrument command, activate CloudWatch Transaction Search, and grant IAM access to CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, and X-Ray. Let's review why. Option A is correct, because the module lists exactly these requirements: the requirements file must include the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry package, you launch the agent using the opentelemetry-instrument command before your Python script, you activate CloudWatch Transaction Search once per account so trace data flows to X-Ray, and you grant IAM permissions for CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, and X-Ray. Option B is incorrect, because enabling observability is not a single console checkbox; the module specifies concrete package, launch, and IAM steps. Option C is incorrect, because observability is built on OpenTelemetry through the AWS Distro, not a proprietary AWS-only tracing agent. Option D is incorrect, because the agent's role does need CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, and X-Ray permissions.

questions.prompt: A team wants to gate a deployment by running evaluations against specific traces in CI/CD before release, and separately to monitor live traffic continuously. Which description of AgentCore Evaluations is correct?
options: Evaluations run only after an agent is retired, as a one-time offline report.

Evaluations uses an LLM-as-a-judge approach with built-in and custom evaluators; on-demand evaluation targets specific spans or traces (suited to CI/CD gating), while online evaluation continuously samples live production traffic.
Evaluations rely solely on exact-match string comparison rather than an LLM judge.
Evaluations operate only at the session level and cannot assess individual tool calls.
questions.answer: Evaluations uses an LLM-as-a-judge approach with built-in and custom evaluators; on-demand evaluation targets specific spans or traces (suited to CI/CD gating), while online evaluation continuously samples live production traffic.
questions.why: The correct answer is B: Evaluations uses an LLM-as-a-judge approach with built-in and custom evaluators; on-demand evaluation targets specific spans or traces, which suits CI/CD gating, while online evaluation continuously samples live production traffic. Let's review why. Option A is incorrect, because evaluations are not a one-time post-retirement report; online evaluation runs continuously on live traffic and on-demand evaluation can run anytime, including before a deployment. Option B is correct, because the module describes Evaluations as using an LLM-as-a-judge technique with built-in and custom evaluators, where on-demand evaluation provides targeted assessment of specified spans or traces by ID, usable for CI/CD regression testing and gating deployments, and online evaluation continuously monitors live production traffic with sampling and filtering. Option C is incorrect, because Evaluations uses an LLM judge, not solely exact-match string comparison. Option D is incorrect, because Evaluations operates at three levels, tool-call, trace, and session, so it can indeed assess individual tool calls.
